newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Conservatives hit by feuding over Europe.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Conservatives hit by feuding over Europe.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major's election campaign was hit by fresh internal feuding over Europe, prompting speculation on Monday that a battle to succeed him as Conservative Party leader had already begun.
The latest opinion poll showed the opposition Labour Party's lead ahead of the May 1 general election had slipped by three points at the weekend to 16 points over the Conservatives.
The Conservatives, however, still seemed unable to get away from the splits over Europe that have plagued their campaign.
Major himself, although insisting confidently that he would win, was ready to discuss what he would do if he lost the election to Labour leader Tony Blair.

In an interview with The Times, Major disclosed that Conservative members of parliament would probably be given a free vote on whether Britain should join a planned single European currency, whatever the election result.
He also said he was willing to give Blair, so far untested in office, the benefit of his experience in negotiating with Britain's partners in the European Union (EU).
"If Tony Blair were prime minister and he asked my advice on how to handle European negotiations, he could have it in complete privacy and in complete frankness," Major said.
Major spoke bitterly about how EU negotiations had led to his disillusionment with Europe,
"My views of Europe have changed with the experience of sitting round the European table.
"It is impossible to sit round the table and not be cynical about the way business is conducted. And I resent that."

Major's growing difficulties in the ruling party were highlighted by a report that a prominent businessman, Paul Sykes, had now contributed more than one million pounds ($1.63 million) of his own money to the campaign funds of anti-European Conservative candidates.
Sykes said 231 candidates had accepted his offer of campaign funds in return for agreeing to defy the government's shaky "negotiate and decide" policy on the single currency.

In one of the most damaging rifts over Europe to emerge during the election campaign, Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke and Home Secretary Michael Howard virtually directly contradicted each other on Sunday.
Howard told Britain's GMTV television that the agenda for the EU summit in Amsterdam in June was "so far-reaching that it would put our survival as a nation state in question".

Clarke, however, told BBC television: "We should not be imagining plots against us. I don't think the survival of Britain as a nation state is at risk because of our membership of the European Union."
Speculation immediately began mounting that some ministers were positioning themselves for a party leadership battle that would follow a Major defeat in the May 1 election.
Labour's finance spokesman Gordon Brown said of the Conservatives: "This is a party that has become two parties...The Conservative leadership campaign has begun."

The Daily Express made Defence Secretary Michael Portillo favourite to succeeed Major, at odds of 4-1, followed by Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine at 5-1 and Howard at 6-1. Clarke was seventh in the betting -- a 16-1 shot. ($1=.6132 Pound)
